description_A:
The module specifies a resource allocator managing a finite set of shared resources among a set of clients. Each client tracks two pieces of state: `unsat`, the set of resources it has outstanding requests for, and `alloc`, the set of resources currently allocated to it. Initially both mappings are empty for every client.

Three actions drive the system. `Request(c,S)` allows client `c` to submit a new request for a nonempty set `S`, but only when it holds no resources and has no pending unsatisfied request. `Allocate(c,S)` lets the allocator grant any nonempty subset of the available (unallocated) resources that overlap the client's outstanding request, partially fulfilling the request if needed. `Return(c,S)` allows a client to return any nonempty subset of its currently held resources, even before its full request has been satisfied.

The principal specification `SimpleAllocator` combines the initial condition and stuttering-closed next-state relation with weak fairness on full returns and strong fairness on allocations. A weaker variant, `SimpleAllocator2`, relaxes the return fairness condition to require returns only after the entire request has been satisfied. The model checks two invariants—`TypeInvariant` and `ResourceMutex` (no two clients hold the same resource simultaneously)—and three liveness properties: `ClientsWillReturn` (clients eventually release resources once satisfied), `ClientsWillObtain` (every requested resource is eventually allocated), and `InfOftenSatisfied` (every client is satisfied infinitely often). The theorems note that the weaker `SimpleAllocator2` preserves `ClientsWillReturn` but not the stronger liveness properties. The model is configured with three clients and two resources.
description_B: This module specifies a simple resource allocator for a finite set of resources and a set of clients. Clients issue requests only when they currently hold no resources and have no outstanding unsatisfied request; requests may then be partially fulfilled over time, and clients may return held resources even before a request is completely satisfied. The specification defines two temporal system specifications with different fairness assumptions, and proves safety and liveness properties such as type correctness, mutual exclusion of resource ownership, eventual return, eventual obtainment, and infinitely often having no unsatisfied requests; it also includes a symmetry expression and a concrete counterexample value structure.

Each process starts in control state "b0" and may individually move to "b1"; once all processes are in "b1", the barrier resets all processes back to "b0" simultaneously. description_B:
The module specifies a cyclic barrier synchronization primitive for N processes. Each process is identified by an integer in the set 1..N, and the single variable `pc` maps each process to one of two program-counter locations, `"b0"` or `"b1"`.

Initially, all processes are at `"b0"`. The action `b0(self)` models an individual process arriving at the barrier: it advances that process's counter from `"b0"` to `"b1"` independently of all others. The action `b1` models the barrier release: it fires only when every process has reached `"b1"`, at which point all processes are simultaneously reset to `"b0"`, allowing the cycle to repeat. The temporal specification is a standard safety specification with no fairness constraints.

Two properties are checked with N set to 6. `TypeOK` is a type invariant confirming that `pc` always maps every process to one of the two valid locations. `BarrierProperty` is a state-machine safety property asserting that no process already past the barrier (at `"b1"`) can leave that state while any other process is still approaching it (at `"b0"`); formally, whenever some process is at `"b0"` and another is at `"b1"`, the latter must remain at `"b1"` in the next step. Together these properties capture the essential barrier guarantee: a process may not proceed past the barrier until all participants have arrived.

description_A:
The module specifies Dijkstra's self-stabilizing token ring algorithm (EWD426). The system models a ring of N nodes, numbered 0 through N−1, each holding a counter variable `c` drawn from the value domain 0 to M−1. The constants N and M must be positive naturals satisfying N ≤ M + 1. A token is not represented explicitly but is instead defined implicitly by relationships among neighboring counters: a unique token exists at position i when all counters before i equal c[0] and all counters from i onward equal (c[0]−1) mod M.

The initial state allows any assignment of counter values in the valid domain, modeling an arbitrary (possibly illegitimate) starting configuration. Two actions drive the system: `CreateToken`, enabled when node 0's counter equals its predecessor's (node N−1), increments c[0] modulo M, injecting a fresh token; and `PassToken(i)`, enabled for any non-zero node i whose counter differs from its predecessor's, copies the predecessor's value, propagating the token around the ring. The overall next-state relation is the disjunction of these two actions, and the temporal specification adds weak fairness over the entire next-state relation. The model checks the invariant `TypeOK`, asserting counters remain in range, and the liveness property `Stab`, which asserts that the system eventually reaches and stays in a state where exactly one token exists in the ring — the classical self-stabilization guarantee. The configuration runs with N = 6 and M = 6 with deadlock checking disabled.
description_B: This specification models Dijkstra's classical self-stabilizing token ring algorithm from EWD426. The system consists of N nodes arranged in a ring, each storing a counter value in a bounded domain 0..M-1; node 0 can create a new token by incrementing relative to the last node, while every other node passes the token by copying its predecessor when their values differ. The spec assumes at least one node and a nonempty value domain, together with the condition N <= M + 1, and it verifies a stabilization property stating that eventually the system reaches and stays in a state with a unique token.

description_A: This module specifies the correctness skeleton of the alternating-bit protocol using sender and receiver bit variables together with sent and received data values. The sender may send a new value when its acknowledgement bit matches its send bit, the receiver may accept a message when its receive bit differs from the sender bit, and the sender may accept an acknowledgement when the receiver bit differs from the sender acknowledgement bit. The specification defines an initial condition, a next-state relation, a type invariant, fairness assumptions for message reception and acknowledgement reception, and a temporal property stating that the sender and acknowledgement bits are infinitely often out of sync.
description_B:
The module ABCorrectness specifies an idealized, channel-free reference model of the Alternating Bit Protocol, intended to capture the correct high-level behavior against which a full implementation can be verified (e.g., via refinement mapping).

The state consists of a sender bit `sBit`, a sender acknowledgement `sAck`, a receiver bit `rBit`, a currently-sent data value `sent`, and a most-recently received data value `rcvd`, all over a finite set `Data` (instantiated as `{d1, d2}`). Initialization allows any consistent starting state where all three bits agree. The action `CSndNewValue` fires when the sender has been acknowledged (`sAck = sBit`), picks a new data value, and flips `sBit` to signal a new transmission. `CRcvMsg` fires when the receiver's bit differs from the sender's, updating `rBit` and copying `sent` into `rcvd` to model successful message delivery. `CRcvAck` fires when the sender's acknowledgement lags behind the receiver's bit, advancing `sAck` to match `rBit`. Weak fairness is required on both `CRcvMsg` and `CRcvAck`, ensuring that pending deliveries and acknowledgements are eventually processed. The specification `ABCSpec` combines initialization, the stuttering-closed next-state relation, and the fairness conditions. The only checked property is the type invariant `TypeInv`, which asserts all bits remain in `{0,1}` and data values stay within `Data`.

description_A: This module models the classic balance-scale stone-cutting problem: given a total weight W and N pieces, find an ordered partition of W into N natural-number weights such that every target weight from 1 to W can be balanced using those pieces on either side of the scale. The specification encodes weighing by allowing coefficients in {-1, 0, 1}, where a negative coefficient represents placing a piece on the same side as the object being weighed. It uses recursive operators to enumerate ordered partitions and to sum sequences, and then uses TLC-oriented ASSUME formulas with PrintT to search for and display a solution or report that no solution exists.
description_B:
The module encodes and solves the Car Talk balance-scale puzzle: given a stone of weight W pounds and a balance scale, find N pieces whose weights allow any integer weight from 1 to W to be measured. Because pieces may be placed on either side of the scale, each piece contributes a coefficient of −1, 0, or +1, so the problem reduces to finding a sequence of N positive integers summing to W such that every integer in 1..W can be expressed as a signed combination of those integers.

The module defines two key operators. `Partitions(seq, wt)` recursively enumerates all non-decreasing sequences of N natural numbers that sum to W, pruning the search using tight bounds on valid element ranges. `Weighs(seq, wt)` checks whether a given partition can represent a target weight by existentially quantifying over coefficient assignments from {−1, 0, 1} applied to each piece. The central `ASSUME` statement directs TLC to search all such ordered partitions and, for each one, test whether every weight in 1..W is achievable; if a valid partition is found, it is printed via `PrintT`; otherwise the string "No solution" is printed. The module has no variables, no state transitions, and no temporal properties — it is purely a model-checking computation wrapper that exploits TLC's assumption-evaluation mechanism to solve a combinatorial puzzle, with the default configuration setting W = 40 and N = 4.

description_A:
The module specifies an N-process shared-memory algorithm that is a variant of a simpler algorithm (from module Simple), modified to use *regular registers* instead of atomic registers. Each process `i` in the range `0..N-1` has a shared register `x[i]`, modeled as a non-empty subset of `{0,1}` to capture the semantics of a regular register, and a local register `y[i]` holding a value in `{0,1}`.

Each process executes three steps: at `a1` it sets `x[self]` to `{0,1}` (representing the transient state during a write of 1 over the old value 0); at `a2` it completes the write by setting `x[self]` to `{1}`; at `b` it reads a nondeterministically chosen value from `x[(self-1) % N]` into `y[self]`, modeling that a regular-register read may return any value currently in the register's value set. The specification `Spec` is the initial condition plus a stuttering-closed next-state relation, with a `Termination` liveness property asserting all processes eventually reach `Done`.

The safety property `PCorrect` asserts that when all processes have finished, at least one process read the value 1. The inductive invariant `Inv` combines a type invariant `TypeOK` with two structural conditions: every process at or past label `b` has already completed its write (`x[i] = {1}`), and either some process is not yet done or some `y[i]` equals 1. Two TLAPS-verified theorems, `Correctness` and `Correctness2`, prove that `Spec` implies `[]PCorrect` using this inductive invariant. The model-checking configuration sets `N = 8` and checks `PCorrect`, `TypeOK`, and `Inv` as invariants.
description_B: This module specifies an N-process shared-memory algorithm in which each process writes its own shared register and then reads a neighbor's register, using regular registers rather than atomic registers for the shared x values. The model represents a regular register by a set of possible values, so a write from 0 to 1 is modeled by first changing a register value from {0} to {0,1} and then to {1}; a read may return any element currently in that set. The specification defines the translated PlusCal actions, an initial condition, the next-state relation, a termination condition, a safety property PCorrect stating that if all processes are done then some y[i] equals 1, an inductive invariant Inv used to prove that property, and two TLAPS proofs establishing correctness.

description_A:
The module specifies a simple concurrent algorithm in which N processes, numbered 0 through N−1 and conceptually arranged in a circle, each execute two sequential steps. In step `a`, process `i` writes 1 into shared array `x` at index `i`. In step `b`, it reads `x` at the left-neighbor index `(i−1) mod N` and writes that value into shared array `y` at index `i`. All processes begin at label `a`, and the PlusCal translation produces variables `x`, `y` (both initialized to all-zeros arrays over {0,1}), and a program-counter array `pc` tracking each process's current label among `{"a", "b", "Done"}`. The constant `N` is assumed to be a positive natural number; the model-checking configuration fixes it to 5.

The core correctness property, `PCorrect`, asserts that when all processes have terminated, at least one process `i` has `y[i] = 1`. The module proves `Spec => []PCorrect` using TLAPS by establishing an inductive invariant `Inv`, which combines type-correctness (`TypeOK`) with two additional conjuncts: that any process past label `a` has already set `x[i] = 1`, and that either some process has not yet finished or some `y[i]` is already 1. Two TLAPS theorems (`Correctness` and `Correctness2`) formally verify this invariance, the latter being a more concise proof accepted by the same proof system. TLC is also configured to check `PCorrect`, `TypeOK`, and `Inv` as invariants against the specification.
description_B: This module specifies a simple concurrent ring algorithm with N processes arranged in a circle. Each process first sets its own x entry to 1, then copies the left neighbor's x value into its own y entry; the specification includes the PlusCal algorithm in comments and its translated TLA+ form with variables x, y, and pc. The model assumes N is a positive natural number, defines the behavior with Init, Next, and Spec, asserts termination as eventual completion of all processes, and proves a safety property stating that when all processes are done, at least one process has y[i] = 1. The file also develops an inductive invariant Inv, includes type correctness constraints, and contains TLAPS proofs of the main correctness theorem in two versions.

description_A: This module specifies a resource allocator for a finite set of clients and resources. Clients issue resource requests only when they have no outstanding unsatisfied request and currently hold no resources; requests may be partially satisfied, resources may be returned early, and a schedule sequence constrains which client requests may be served before others. The specification includes weak fairness assumptions requiring clients to return resources once fully satisfied, requiring allocations to eventually happen when enabled, and requiring scheduling to eventually occur; it states and checks type, mutual exclusion, allocator invariants, and several liveness properties such as eventual return, eventual obtainment of requested resources, and infinitely often satisfied requests.
description_B:
The module specifies a scheduling-based resource allocator that manages a shared pool of resources among a set of competing clients. Three variables track the system state: `unsat`, mapping each client to its current set of outstanding (unsatisfied) resource requests; `alloc`, mapping each client to the resources currently allocated to it; and `sched`, a sequence of clients representing the current allocation schedule.

Four actions define the next-state relation. `Request` allows a client with no pending requests and no held resources to submit a new non-empty resource request. `Schedule` non-deterministically appends a permutation of all currently unscheduled clients with pending requests to the end of the schedule sequence. `Allocate` grants a subset of available, requested resources to a client that appears in the schedule, provided no client appearing earlier in the schedule has requested any of those resources; when a client's request is fully satisfied it is removed from the schedule. `Return` allows a client to release any subset of its held resources at any time, even before its full request is met, though clients are only obligated to return resources once fully satisfied.

Liveness conditions require weak fairness of full returns when a client's request is satisfied, weak fairness of any partial allocation for each client, and weak fairness of scheduling. The module asserts six theorems: type correctness, mutual exclusion of allocated resources, a structural allocator invariant ensuring schedulability, and three liveness properties — that clients eventually return all resources, that every requested resource is eventually allocated, and that every client is infinitely often fully satisfied. The model-checking configuration instantiates three clients and two resources and checks all invariants and liveness properties.
